body.text: When part of a glacier collapsed above the Lhende Khola on August 26, the debris flow it triggered was initially mistaken by the US Geological Survey’s automated network for a magnitude-4.4 earthquake. By August 31, the combined toll in Nepal and China’s Tibet had climbed to around 900 dead, with more than 4,000 people still missing, including, as per Nepal’s Independent Power Producers’ Association, nearly 900 hydropower workers feared trapped in tunnels.

Nepal’s Finance Minister has said the country will need $4-5 billion to rebuild, which is nearly a tenth of its economy. The collapse itself occurred on the Nepali side of the border, on Langtang Lirung, but the debris fell into the Lhende Khola river system spanning the Nepal-China border, and the resulting flood surged downstream through Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts within a day. Further downstream, rising river levels prompted India to begin evacuations in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, and Uttarakhand. Given that South Asia’s hazards cross borders frequently, the question is why the region’s institutions still don’t.

South Asia’s problem is not a shortage of paper. As far back as 2005, in the aftermath of the Indian Ocean tsunami, SAARC’s Dhaka Declaration underscored the urgency of a “permanent regional response mechanism dedicated to disaster preparedness, emergency relief and rehabilitation”. A Comprehensive Framework on Disaster Management followed in 2006, promising shared early-warning and cross-border data exchange. A Rapid Response mechanism signed after Pakistan’s 2010 floods did not come into force until 2016; most provisions remain unimplemented.

SAARC has not held a summit since 2014, after the 2016 Islamabad summit collapsed when India and the others stayed away following the Uri attack. The same body that diagnosed the problem two decades ago has been unable to hold its own annual meetings, leave alone run a real-time data-sharing mechanism. Meanwhile, India, Bangladesh, and the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC) bloc have built bilateral and subregional mechanisms. But if SAARC has failed, why do the mechanisms that grew up around it still remain disconnected?

Let us separate the components of “disaster cooperation”. South Asia’s institutions handle its four components unevenly. Monitoring asks what is happening upstream. Data-sharing asks who else learns about it and how fast. Warning asks who tells downstream governments and populations. Response asks who is permitted to physically enter another country’s territory to help.
The region does not lack instruments for any of these individually. What it lacks is a chain connecting them: monitoring to data-sharing, data-sharing to warning, and warning to response.
The precedents nobody heeded

The clearest warning came 18 years ago, when the eastern Kosi embankment breached at Kushaha in Nepal in August 2008. The water scholar Ajaya Dixit recorded that some 50,000 people in Nepal and some 3.5 million people in Bihar were affected. The 1966 Kosi treaty had left embankment maintenance and monitoring without a clearly defined bilateral operational channel. Along with inadequate embankment maintenance on the Nepali side and the scale of the breach, the treaty’s silence on how to operationalise cooperation meant that there was no fast bilateral mechanism to turn a warning into downstream evacuation. Nine years later, the 2017 monsoon flooded India, Nepal, and Bangladesh, affecting an estimated 41 million people, but the response was similar.

In October 2023, Sikkim’s South Lhonak glacial lake, flagged by researchers as having a 42 per cent probability of bursting, did burst, sending a 20-metre wave that destroyed the Teesta-III dam and travelled 385 kilometres into Bangladesh. India’s forecasters alerted Bangladesh the same day, but the early warning system was still a year behind schedule. In other words, it was an Indian gap in preparedness rather than a cross-border cooperation failure, but that only makes the argument stronger. It shows that the problem is at every layer: domestic monitoring, bilateral data exchange, cross-border warning transmission, and coordinated response.

Against that backdrop, this week’s response looks familiar. China’s Premier Li Qiang travelled to the affected Gyirong sector within a day; India sent relief flights and medical teams within 48 hours. Kathmandu initially said its own security agencies would handle search-and-rescue, but within a day, facing pressure, it agreed to accept limited foreign expertise for tunnel rescue, DNA testing, and forensic work.

The External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar described India’s aid as a range of support that Nepal can pick up as it sees fit, negotiated fresh rather than activated from a standing protocol. India has good reason to prefer request-based assistance over an automatic trigger: Nepal’s consent matters for security-linked deployments. Sovereignty and flexibility are genuine constraints, but it would be worth exploring whether pre-negotiating the aid components (tunnelling teams, DNA units, bridging equipment) so that they reach in hours, not days, can be worked out within a consent-based model.

South Asia is not without working models. Since 1972, India and Bangladesh have used their Joint Rivers Commission (JRC) to share daily water-level, discharge, and rainfall data on the Ganges, Brahmaputra, and Teesta, extending the annual sharing window in 2022. Bangladeshi officials argue that it stops short of real-time forecasting on smaller rivers and that political friction is stalling the broader agenda. The JRC’s 1996 Ganges Water Sharing Treaty expires in December 2026, and in February 2026 the government told the Lok Sabha that renewal talks had not yet begun, despite a parliamentary panel urging the government to open them “without further delay”.

Separately, India’s National Disaster Management Authority has hosted BIMSTEC’s Disaster Management Exercises since 2017, with further rounds in 2020, 2021, and a virtual meet in July 2025. Yet that architecture did not translate into a comparable regional deployment when a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck Myanmar in March 2025. The bloc convened a summit in Bangkok, while India separately launched Operation Brahma. A Centre of Excellence for Disaster Management was proposed at BIMSTEC’s own summit weeks later, but the bloc appears to be rehearsing interoperability faster than institutionalising it. There is existing capacity, but nations are failing to merge it into one operational chain.
The China question

India and China do have a channel, the Expert-Level Mechanism on trans-border rivers, established in 2006, meant to meet annually and handle exactly this kind of flood-season data exchange. But the record shows how fragile the arrangement is. According to statements made in Parliament, the Sutlej hydrological-data MoU expired in November 2020 and the Brahmaputra MoU in June 2023; neither has been renewed. China suspended Brahmaputra data-sharing during the 2017 Doklam standoff, citing damage to hydrological stations; reports said the same data continued to reach Bangladesh in that period.

The Sutlej mechanism showed what operational regional cooperation looks like, but such systems stall when inter-nation relations sour and expired MoUs go unrenewed. Now, there are signs of a thaw: days before the Lhende Khola collapse, India and China agreed to hold the next Expert-Level Mechanism meeting in September and to communicate on renewing the lapsed MoUs. This comes one year after China agreed to “give full play” to the mechanism and share hydrological data in emergencies “based on humanitarian considerations”.

There is documentation of a comparable early-warning mechanism between Nepal and China for glacial-lake and landslide hazards, like the one that produced this week’s flood, but China did directly warn Nepal about a new barrier-lake risk in the flood’s immediate aftermath. The India-China record shows not the absence of a mechanism, but one whose continuity has been vulnerable to bilateral relations rather than insulated from it by disasters. This fragility can be fixed by a standing regional protocol.

The various episodes show that South Asia’s problem is not a shortage of existing frameworks but the failure to operationalise them. Agreements are signed after each disaster, but left dormant, or allowed to expire, until the next disaster strikes. Seen from a realistic perspective, what the region needs is not a new institution, but narrower and more focussed measures: data-sharing protocols renewed regularly; pre-cleared technical-assistance protocols that activate within hours; and jointly-funded glacial-lake monitoring, most plausibly starting between India and Nepal who already cooperate bilaterally, and with a separate and slower track toward bringing China into a Nepal-facing early-warning arrangement. This still leaves the harder questions unanswered: who pays, who owns the sensors, who certifies risk, who has authority to issue a warning, or cross a border to act on one.

The scale of the monitoring gap is on record: the Indian government said in July 2026 that it monitors 2,485 glacial lakes and has scientifically assessed 189 high-risk ones in 2025, 56 of them very high risk. This includes an autonomous profiling and risk-assessment system handed over to Sikkim in June 2026. What remains now is to turn that information into interoperable, downstream warnings that can cross administrative and national borders. South Asia’s governments increasingly know which lakes are dangerous, but they must now build the chain that can convert knowledge into pre-warning systems for downstream action.

The ice and rock that collapsed above the Lhende Khola did not respect borders. South Asia’s governments must build disaster-response institutions with the same disregard for borders. Without that, every few years they will continue to be taken unawares by the next flood and the next landslide.
